questions.prompt: Explain the two separate decisions every ticket request goes through, why the role check lives in the service, and where the weak half is.

keyPoints.text: The auth middleware only establishes identity; it does not decide permissions.
keyPoints.quote: It does not decide what that user may do.

keyPoints.text: A viewer's PATCH is refused by the service after nothing more than the user lookup.
keyPoints.quote: the service refuses it, after only the auth lookup of the user row

keyPoints.text: Putting the check in the service protects every caller, not just HTTP routes.
keyPoints.quote: Because the check is in the service rather than the route, it also holds for a test, a script or a future worker

keyPoints.text: Identity itself is weak: the email header is just a claim.
keyPoints.quote: The email header is an unverified claim

keyPoints.text: The fix for identity is a real session or token check in front of the middleware, leaving the rest unchanged.
keyPoints.quote: Production would put a session or token check in front of

keyPoints.text: The service gate runs on the first line of updateTicket.

questions.prompt: How does the code keep tenants apart and keep internal notes away from viewers, and what makes each of those rules fragile?

keyPoints.text: Tenant scope in the lookup makes a foreign id indistinguishable from a missing one.
keyPoints.quote: makes a foreign id behave like a missing one, so the response does not reveal that the id exists elsewhere

keyPoints.text: There is no database-level enforcement; the service predicate is the only tenant guard.
keyPoints.quote: The schema has no row-level security; the service is the only thing selecting the right tenant.

keyPoints.text: The update itself has no tenant predicate and relies on the earlier scoped read.
keyPoints.quote: It is safe only because the tenant-scoped read

keyPoints.text: Before the repair, GET and PATCH disagreed about internal notes.
keyPoints.quote: So GET hid the note and the PATCH response carried it.

keyPoints.text: The general rule: any endpoint that returns the resource is a read path.
keyPoints.quote: every endpoint that returns a ticket is a read path, including the ones whose verb is a write

keyPoints.text: One role-aware include now feeds both call sites.

questions.prompt: What do the transaction and the Serializable retry wrapper guarantee for a ticket update, and what do they not cover?

keyPoints.text: The ticket update, audit row and outbox row are one atomic unit.
keyPoints.quote: so they commit together or not at all

keyPoints.text: The outbox row is a stored promise that a notification will be sent later.
keyPoints.quote: The outbox row is a durable promise to notify.

keyPoints.text: Because notifications only follow committed rows, a rolled-back change never announces itself.
keyPoints.quote: a rolled-back change can never have announced itself

keyPoints.text: Serializable failures are expected and must be retried by the application.
keyPoints.quote: the contract is that the application retries

keyPoints.text: Only serialization failures are retried; a unique violation would just fail again.
The transition is validated on a read made before the transaction, which Serializable cannot protect.
keyPoints.quote: Serializable protects the reads made inside the transaction, and the transaction makes none.

keyPoints.text: The retry wrapper re-runs the callback up to three times on P2034 only.
